summary:
Egypt's immigration law gives the Ministry of Interior broad authority to refuse entry to, or order the removal of, anyone deemed to disturb public order or morality. The Cairo 52 study 'Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here' (27 November 2023) analyses that statute and the case law built on it alongside 12 documented incidents from 2018 to 2022, and finds the power applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans in cases where no charge was ever upheld. Removal does not require a conviction, or any offence at all, under Egyptian law.

No penal provision names homosexual conduct. Prosecutions proceed instead through the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961, whose Article 9(C) the Economic Courts have read together with Penal Code provisions; Cairo 52 reported on 24 January 2024 that this marks a shift from de facto to explicit criminalisation. Court of Cassation rulings in the 1970s had already stripped out the requirement of financial exchange, holding that habitual or multiple partners were sufficient. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, describes public-morality and debauchery provisions being used routinely for arrests that carry prison sentences.

Police entrapment through dating apps is documented. A BBC investigation found officers running fake profiles on apps used by LGBT people, with victims describing blackmail and arrest; no explicit homosexuality statute was needed because the debauchery law supplied the charge. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights documents the same method aimed particularly at transgender women, through fake accounts on dating apps and websites, and records violations continuing inside police stations.

Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing records coerced anal examinations alongside rising arrests of gay and trans people, and states that the authorities turn a blind eye. Forced anal testing was also used on those detained in the 2017 crackdown.

Sentencing exposure attached to online activity is severe. In 2004 a seventeen-year-old private university student received a seventeen-year prison sentence, including two years' hard labour, for posting a personal profile on a gay dating site.

Health care is a further barrier. TIMEP, in a 6 January 2025 submission for Egypt's fourth Universal Periodic Review cycle, reports that transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices that violate the right to health, and that barriers to equitable health services have persisted since the previous review, with pervasive discrimination on grounds of gender identity and sexual orientation in healthcare.

Personal status and family law follow the religious law of the person's recognised religion, and Egyptian law recognises marriage only between a man and a woman. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status should assume no recognition, and should assume that if the relationship becomes known to police it may be treated as evidence in an indictment under provisions against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality.

No law or policy prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression or sex characteristics, as recorded by Outright International and Bedayaa. State officials and police routinely harass, abuse and torture LGBT people, particularly trans people, producing arrests that do not hold up and abuse in custody.

Pew Research Center polling found that 95% of Egyptians believe homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and no political party or human rights NGO expresses public support for LGBT rights.
tangentialFactors:
Expression is separately policed. In 2017 the Supreme Media Regulatory Council issued an order preventing 'the appearance of the homosexuals' or 'promoting their slogans' in media, and in August 2018 the government introduced legislation placing any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws. In 2013 the Morsi government charged the comedian Bassem Youssef with 'propagating and promoting homosexuality and obscenity'. In January 2019 the television host Mohamed El Gheity was jailed for one year for hosting a gay man on his programme, and in 2009 the newspaper Al Balagh Al Gadid was shut down with two reporters jailed over a story about actors and homosexual prostitution.

Earlier crackdowns establish the pattern. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report 'In a Time of Torture' documents the Queen Boat-era campaign, including arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings over sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants. In December 2014 the television presenter Mona Iraqi worked with police to raid a public bathhouse, around 26 men were arrested, and they were later acquitted. After the September 2017 rainbow flag incident, the television hosts Ahmed Moussa and Mohamed Al Gheity repeatedly incited violence against the community; Moussa published personal information of those who had raised the flag, and at least 84 people were arrested between 25 September and the end of November 2017, many of them subjected to forced anal tests.

The aftermath of that period was severe for Egyptian LGBT people. The September 2017 crackdown produced trauma and despair among young Egyptians, with many attempting suicide. Sarah Hegazi, detained for three months after the incident, fled the country, was granted asylum in Canada and died by suicide in 2020. Many Egyptian LGBT people left the country under social and political pressure. Visibility increased after the 2011 revolution and online campaigns against homophobia and transphobia spread in 2013, but this produced no legal reform.

The word 'khawalat', historically applied to male cross-dressing dancers, has been stigmatised and is used as a derogatory term for passive and gay men.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition is being closed off. A Ministry of Interior directive to civil-registry heads nationwide ends the route under the Civil Status Law 143/1994 that allowed transgender Egyptians to correct their gender markers through governorate committees, as reported by Cairo 52 on 12 December 2024.

Egyptian nationals carry the same enforcement exposure without the option of leaving. Bedayaa records rising arrests of gay and trans Egyptians, and the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights documents entrapment aimed particularly at transgender women. Detention conditions and the position of trans people inside the country are documented in Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing as a reference for work on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics.

Family and personal status law is organised by the religious law of the person's recognised religion, whether Islam or Coptic Orthodox Christianity, and none of those systems recognises a relationship between two people of the same sex. Egyptian law therefore recognises marriage only between a man and a woman, and a relationship that becomes public can be used as evidence in a criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 12 incidents from 2018 to 2022 cited by Cairo 52 are not itemised in the source, and no breakdown by nationality, point of entry or outcome is available.

No consolidated official figures exist for arrests, prosecutions or deportations under the morality and debauchery provisions. The counts that circulate come from NGO and press documentation and cover specific windows, such as the 84 arrests recorded between 25 September and the end of November 2017.

Whether the immigration powers are exercised at ports of entry, as opposed to inside the country, is not separately documented in the sources reviewed.

The Human Rights Watch material dates from 2004 and describes the Queen Boat period; it evidences a pattern rather than current practice. The 2017 media order and the 2018 social-media legislation are reported without published enforcement statistics. The 2014 bathhouse case ended in acquittals and the source does not record the legal basis for them.
